name: Maca root

card.summary: An Andean root vegetable sold as a libido and energy supplement; a small number of trials suggest possible benefit for sexual desire, with limited evidence overall.
card.note: A systematic review described evidence as limited; a French agency warned about possible health risks of powdered root, which others dispute.

quick.overview:
Maca is a radish-like root grown at high altitude in the Peruvian Andes, eaten as food for centuries and now sold worldwide as powder, capsules and extracts. It is marketed for libido, energy and fertility.

A 2010 systematic review found four randomized trials, with two reporting improved sexual desire or function, one reporting an effect in men with erectile dysfunction and one finding no effect in cyclists; its authors called the evidence limited. A 2026 review reports improved libido in men-only and mixed-sex studies and inconsistent results in women.
quick.mechanism: The mechanism is not established. Maca does not appear to contain hormones; proposed actives include glucosinolates, macamides and alkaloids such as imidazoles, and Wikipedia notes that no pharmacokinetic data have been published.
quick.risks: Maca has a long record as food in the Andes. Wikipedia notes extracts contain MTCA, a compound that may act as an MAO inhibitor, and that France's food-safety agency warned consumers about powdered root, a concern others dispute on the grounds that boiling deactivates it.

lead: Maca (Lepidium meyenii) is a biennial plant of the cabbage family grown at roughly 3,800 to 4,400 meters in the high Andes of Peru, cultivated for its fleshy hypocotyl-taproot, which is eaten as food and sold dried, as flour, or as extract.[1][2] In supplement markets it is promoted for energy, stamina, libido and 'hormonal balance', and it appears in many men's testosterone and sexual-health blends.[3][4]

For appearance, maca is usually taken as part of a physique and vitality routine. The chain people describe runs from more energy, drive and stamina, to more consistent training and better mood, to a better physique; some also take it for the libido and fertility effects reported in small trials. Wikipedia describes traditional medicinal claims as unproven, and a 2010 systematic review of four randomized trials concluded the evidence for sexual function was limited.[1][5] A 2020 review documents its composition and reported effects on sexual dysfunction, memory, mood, antioxidant and skin-protection activity.[8]
Archaeological evidence shows cultivation around Lake Junín from about 1700 BC, Spanish chroniclers described it in the early 1600s, and commercial interest grew from the late 1980s.[1]

paras: Maca is the only member of its genus with a fleshy hypocotyl, forms a low rosette of leaves, is largely self-pollinating and has 64 chromosomes.[1] It tolerates frost and thin soils, is cultivated largely without synthetic inputs, and is harvested by hand.[1] The species was named by Walpers in 1843; some researchers argue for a separate species, Lepidium peruvianum, though most botanists keep L. meyenii.[1]

Traditional growers recognise colour varieties such as cream-yellow, half-purple, purple and black, with colour linked to anthocyanin pigments.[1] A 2024 review notes that up to seventeen colours (phenotypes) have been described and that colour, root size, growing location and post-harvest processing can change the nutrient and phytochemical profile, while research separating the colours by clinical use remains limited.[9]

Traditionally the root is roasted, boiled into porridge or juice, or fermented into a weak beer, and in Andean communities it is eaten in quantities exceeding 20 grams per day.[1][2] Supplement products use dried or gelatinized powder or concentrated extracts.[1] One DailyMed-listed product combines maca extract with tongkat ali and sea buckthorn.[4]

In looksmaxxing and men's-health settings it sits in the 'testosterone booster' and vitality category and is marketed for libido, energy and mood.[3][4] A 2024 systematic review of testosterone boosters covered 52 studies of 27 proposed products, two of them on maca, and reported that most boosters did not raise total testosterone in the populations studied.[11] In a 12-week randomized trial in healthy men, maca improved self-reported sexual desire without changing serum testosterone or estradiol.[12]

Maca is mostly carbohydrate by dry weight and contains glucosinolates, polyphenols, imidazole alkaloids and macamides, a group of fatty-acid amides named for the plant.[1][7][10] A 2003 Journal of Natural Products paper reported imidazole alkaloids isolated from the root.[7] A 2024 review notes that chemical composition varies with ecotype, growing conditions and processing.[10]
Wikipedia notes that no pharmacokinetic data have been published, and that maca extracts contain MTCA, a compound that may act as a monoamine oxidase inhibitor and possible mutagen.[1]

A 2010 systematic review (Shin and colleagues) identified four randomized controlled trials: two reported positive effects on sexual desire or dysfunction, one found no effect in healthy cyclists and one reported significant effects in men with erectile dysfunction. The authors described the evidence as limited and called for more rigorous studies.[5]

Individual trials include a 12-week double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of gelatinized maca in healthy men aged 21 to 56, which found improved sexual desire from week 8 with no difference in testosterone or estradiol versus placebo;[12] a 2003 randomized trial of serum reproductive hormones in healthy men;[16] a double-blind trial in men with mild erectile dysfunction that examined subjective well-being and sexual performance;[14] and randomized trials in infertile men examining seminal quality and fertility outcomes.[13][15]

A 2025 double-blind crossover study examined maca supplementation on basketball-related performance and antifatigue ability.[17] A 2016 systematic review is described by Wikipedia as suggesting improved semen quality, and a 2011 review found the evidence for menopausal symptoms inconclusive.[1] A 2026 review reported that maca appeared to improve libido in studies of men and mixed-sex groups, that results in women (often postmenopausal) were inconsistent, and that most trials used about 3 g per day of powder.[5]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists trials of maca in male sexual dysfunction, postmenopausal sexual function, antidepressant-induced sexual dysfunction, and exercise performance in basketball and badminton players, several with small samples.[6][19][20] A 2016 review of polyphenols and sunburn included a study of maca among its sources of polyphenols.[18]

A 2024 review states that maca is generally regarded as safe with rare adverse effects, citing preclinical low toxicity and good human tolerance in clinical studies.[10] Wikipedia notes that France's food-safety agency warned consumers about powdered root because of MTCA, while others argued that boiling deactivates it.[1]

Cultivation evidence near Lake Junín dates to about 1700 BC.[1] Antonio Vázquez de Espinosa described maca about 1598; it was traded for lowland staples and used to pay Spanish colonial taxes.[1] Cultivation was limited to the Junín area until the late 1980s, when it was commercially rediscovered on the Meseta de Bombón, and export interest grew from the 1990s.[1] In 2014 Peruvian institutions accused Chinese companies of illegally exporting maca and of biopiracy through patents related to maca propagation.[1]
Maca is sold as a food and dietary supplement, not as a drug.[1] A review of sexual-enhancement products for sale online lists it among the ingredients of such supplements.[3]

angle.text: Maca is taken by people who want more energy and drive for training and, in men's supplement stacks, support for libido. Small randomized trials have examined sexual desire, semen quality and exercise performance; the link to physique is the one users draw.
